title: Human impact on environments
keyIdea: People change the places where plants and animals live. Habitat destruction, such as deforestation, and pollution take away homes and food, so biodiversity falls and some species become endangered or even extinct. Burning fossil fuels (coal, oil and gas) is non-renewable and adds carbon dioxide to the air; your carbon footprint measures how much your choices add. Conservation, renewable energy and sustainable choices help protect habitats for the future.
familyTip: Walk round your local park or garden and count how many different kinds of plant, bird and minibeast you can spot. Then count the kinds on a mown lawn. Which patch has more biodiversity? At home, talk about one trip each week you could walk or cycle instead of going by car.

visual.caption: Does it harm habitats or help protect them? Drag each card to a box, or tap the card then a box.

items: Cutting down a rainforest for farmland (deforestation)
Plastic bags blowing into the sea (pollution)
Protecting a wood as a nature reserve (conservation)
Walking to school instead of going by car

lab.caption: Flagship lab: count kinds in a wood and a field, cut and replant trees, keep litter out of a river, sort energy sources, shrink a carbon footprint.

kid: Biodiversity means how many different kinds of living thing live in a place. A wood with owls, bees, mushrooms and flowers has lots of biodiversity. A field of only wheat has very little, even if it has a million plants.

A habitat is the home where a plant or animal finds food and shelter. When people cut down forests, it is called deforestation. Animals lose their homes. If a kind of animal has only a few left, it is endangered. If every last one dies, it is extinct, and it can never come back.

Pollution is harmful stuff getting into the air, water or land. Litter dropped on the ground can be washed into rivers by rain and hurt fish. Coal, oil and gas are fossil fuels. They took millions of years to form, so they will run out. They are non-renewable. Sun, wind and moving water will never run out. They are renewable.

Burning fossil fuels puts carbon dioxide gas into the air, and that warms the planet. Your carbon footprint is how much carbon dioxide is made because of the things you do. Walking, cycling and saving energy make it smaller. Living in a way that does not use up the Earth is called sustainability. Protecting habitats is called conservation.
adult: Ages 8 to 11. This topic is about using the words for human impact precisely. Biodiversity is the variety of living things in a place. It counts different species, not individuals, so a big field of one crop has low biodiversity. WWF's Living Planet Report names habitat loss, including deforestation, as the biggest cause of wildlife decline. Pollution, overuse and climate change add to it.

Endangered means a species is at serious risk of dying out. Extinct means none are left anywhere; the dodo was last seen in the 1600s. Conservation protects or restores habitats and species, for example with nature reserves, replanting and breeding programmes.

Renewable sources, such as sunlight, wind and moving water, are replaced naturally as we use them. Fossil fuels formed from ancient living things over millions of years, so they are non-renewable. Burning them releases carbon dioxide, the main gas behind climate change. A carbon footprint is the total of these gases caused by what a person does, usually given in kilograms of carbon dioxide. Sustainability means meeting our needs without harming the future.

Common mistakes: counting lots of one plant as high biodiversity; thinking animals just move to the trees that are left; mixing up endangered and extinct; calling coal renewable because it came from plants; and reading 'carbon footprint' as a real footprint or as rubbish. The lab's travel figures use the UK government's 2023 factors: about 0.17 kg of carbon dioxide per km by car and 0.1 kg per person per km by local bus. So a 4 km school day is about 0.7 kg by car and 0.4 kg by bus.

practice.prompt: Which place has the most biodiversity?
choices: A hedge with 30 different kinds of plant and animal
A field with 5,000 wheat plants
A car park with one tree
practice.hint: Biodiversity counts different kinds, not how many of one kind.
practice.explain: The hedge has 30 different kinds. The wheat field has thousands of plants but only 1 kind.

practice.prompt: A wood had {=a} kinds of bird. After deforestation, {=b} kinds lost their homes and left. How many kinds of bird are left?
practice.hint: Take the kinds that left away from the kinds there were.
practice.explain: {=a} − {=b} = {=a-b}. Only {=a-b} kinds are left, so biodiversity has fallen.

practice.prompt: Which of these is a fossil fuel?
choices: Oil
Wind
Sunlight
practice.hint: Fossil fuels formed from things that lived millions of years ago.
practice.explain: Oil, coal and natural gas are fossil fuels. They are non-renewable because they took millions of years to form.

practice.prompt: A family's car trips add {=k} kg of carbon dioxide to the air each week. How many kg is that in 4 weeks?
practice.hint: Multiply the amount for one week by 4.
practice.explain: {=k} × 4 = {=k*4} kg. That is part of the family's carbon footprint.

choices: There are none left alive anywhere
There are only a few left
It has moved to a new habitat
practice.hint: Think of the dodo or the dinosaurs.
practice.explain: Extinct means every last one has died, so that kind can never come back. 'Only a few left' is endangered.

choices: Cutting down large areas of forest
Planting new forests
Animals moving out of a forest
pool.hint: 'De' at the start of a word often means taking away, as in 'defrost'.
pool.explain: Deforestation is clearing forests, often for farms or building. It destroys habitats.

pool.prompt: What does a carbon footprint measure?
choices: How much carbon dioxide is added to the air by what you do
How big your feet are
How much rubbish you throw away
pool.hint: It is about a gas, not a real footprint.
pool.explain: It adds up the carbon dioxide made by your travel, heating, food and things you buy.

choices: Wind
Coal
Natural gas
pool.hint: Which one will never run out?
pool.explain: The wind keeps blowing however much we use it. Coal and gas are fossil fuels and will run out.

pool.prompt: A species has only 50 animals left in the wild. Which word fits best?
choices: Endangered
Extinct
Renewable
pool.hint: Some are still alive, but very few.
pool.explain: Endangered means at risk of dying out. Extinct would mean none left at all.

pool.prompt: Litter is dropped in a park far from the river. Why can it still harm the river?
choices: Rain and wind can carry it into the water
It cannot, it stays in the park
Litter turns into fish food
pool.hint: Remember what the rain did in the lab.
pool.explain: Rain washes litter into drains and streams, and wind blows it about. It ends up polluting rivers and the sea.

pool.prompt: Volunteers plant {=r} trees every weekend to help a wood recover. How many trees do they plant in {=w} weekends?
pool.hint: Multiply trees per weekend by the number of weekends.
pool.explain: {=r} × {=w} = {=r*w} trees. Replanting and protecting habitats is conservation.

pool.prompt: Which choice is the most sustainable?
choices: Mending a broken toy instead of buying a new one
Buying a new toy every week
Throwing toys away when they get dirty
pool.hint: Sustainable means it could go on without using up the Earth.
pool.explain: Mending uses no new materials or energy to make a new toy, so it can go on for ever.

pool.prompt: Why is coal non-renewable even though it came from plants?
choices: It took millions of years to form, so it will run out
Plants are not alive
Coal grows back each year
pool.hint: How long does it take for new coal to form?
pool.explain: Coal formed from plants buried millions of years ago. We use it far faster than it can form.

choices: Protecting habitats and the living things in them
Using up fossil fuels
Counting how many animals there are
pool.hint: In the lab, what happened when you planted the trees back?
pool.explain: Conservation means protecting and restoring habitats, like nature reserves and replanting woods.

pool.prompt: A patch of rainforest had {=t} hundred trees. Loggers cut down {=c} hundred of them. How many hundred trees are left?
pool.hint: Take the trees cut down away from the trees there were.
pool.explain: {=t} − {=c} = {=t-c}, so {=t-c} hundred trees are left. Every tree lost is a lost home for animals.
